title: Kavishri, voice alone
hookLine: unaccompanied sung poetry about Sikh history

cards: Take away the drum. Take away the fiddle, the harmonium, the tabla. What's left?
A few singers standing close together, one with a hand cupped by one ear, voices racing through verse at a speed that leaves the crowd breathless, rhymes landing like footsteps on a wooden floor.
No instrument to lean on, nothing to hide behind. If a singer loses the beat, everybody hears it. This is sung poetry with nothing but the human voice, and it tells the same history the dhadis tell.

teach.b: First, the name. Kavishri is the art of the kavishar, the poet-singer.

teach.h: THE BEAT LIVES IN THE WORDS.
teach.b: A kavishri group sings without instruments: one voice leads, the others answer and join, and the poetry itself carries the beat. Second, how a voice keeps time alone.
Without a drum, the rhythm has to live inside the words. Kavishri verse is built in tight meters, with rhymes that come back on schedule, so the line drives itself forward.
The singers breathe together, cut off together, and push the pace together: a kind of athletic poetry. Third, what it sings.

teach.h: THE PANTH'S HISTORY, ON BARE BREATH.
teach.b: Like the dhadis, kavishars sing the panth's history: the Gurus, the martyrs, the brave and the faithful, at gurdwara gatherings and at fairs where people come to remember. The story arrives fast, on bare breath.
Fourth, why a bare voice is enough. The third pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak's morning prayer, is a picture of people singing.

teach.h: SOME SING OF POWER, SOME OF GIFTS.
teach.b: In paraphrase: some sing of God's power, if they have the power to sing it; some sing of God's gifts, and know them as signs; some sing of God's glories and greatness; and still the telling never runs out.
Each sings with whatever gift they were given; no one in that picture waits for the right equipment.
A kavishar is a living version of that line: a poet, a breath, and a story worth telling, with nothing in the hands at all.

how: Kavishri groups sing Sikh history in fast, rhymed verse without instruments, one voice leading and the others joining, at gurdwara gatherings and fairs.

o: poetry written down to be read in silence
a festival dance performed to drum music
Sikh history sung fast with no instruments

p: some sing of power, some of gifts

s: kavishri is sung with a drum and a fiddle
that's the dhadis. kavishri is the voice alone.
in kavishri the rhythm is carried by the poetry itself
tight meters and returning rhymes drive the line forward.
Japji's third pauri pictures people singing with whatever gift they have
some sing of power, some of gifts; still the telling never runs out.

games.q: you're a kavishar and the crowd is waiting, but no one has brought a single instrument. what do you do?
o: sing anyway; the beat lives in the words.
read the poem quietly from paper.
games.why: kavishri never needed the drum: the voices lead and answer, and the poetry carries the beat.

practice: Say a few lines you know by heart out loud, slowly: a hymn, a verse from childhood, any poem that has stayed with you.

Then say them again a little faster and find their beat with nothing but your own breath; if you'd rather stay silent, mouth the words, feel the rhythm in your chest, and sit in the quiet after the last line.
